index.html:
- Welcome. This session is about how Elastic is redefining observability for the AI era — from datastore to autonomous SRE.
- One sentence to hold onto: observability is no longer about watching dashboards. It's about systems that understand and fix themselves.
- We'll go from the platform, through the three pillars, and finish with Ninghtshift — the AI SRE.
00-portfolio.html:
- Quick grounding on who we are: the Search AI Company. One platform, three products.
- The foundation is Elasticsearch — search and analytics engine, vector database, AI index, ES|QL. Everything else is built on top of it.
- Observability is one of the three solutions: logs, metrics, traces at AI scale — with an AI SRE agent built in.
- The point: observability isn't a bolt-on for us. It inherits everything the platform can do.
fy27-pillars.html:
- Our answer, in three pillars — and they build on each other.
- Streams: the telemetry pipeline. Open-standard ingestion at any scale — OTel, Prometheus, anything.
- Signals: every observability experience unified — logs, metrics, traces, synthetics, profiles.
- Elastic nightshift: the autonomous AI SRE that sits on top.
- Data in, experiences on top, intelligence above. Keep that structure — the rest of the deck follows it.
streams-intro.html:
- Pillar one: Streams. Five stages, one pipeline — every signal from any source to Elasticsearch.
- Edge collection: run what you already have — Elastic Agent, OTel Collector, Fluent Bit, Logstash, Prometheus exporters. No lock-in.
- Managed inputs: fully hosted endpoints — OTLP, Prometheus, cloud sources. No agent to run at all.
- The message: we meet your data wherever it lives. Zero re-instrumentation.
13-otel-collection.html:
- OpenTelemetry is the strategy, not a checkbox. We're the #1 OTel contributor.
- EDOT — the Elastic Distribution of OpenTelemetry — collects everything, from everywhere: cloud, on-prem, or mixed.
- Note the Cloud Forwarder and Managed Integrations: EDOT as a function — no infra, triggers on cloud events.
- Standardize on OTel without sacrificing analytics depth. That's the promise.
06-streams.html:
- This is Streams end-to-end: from raw data to immediate insight. Always up-to-date, real-time, zero configuration.
- Any source, any format on the left — OTLP, Kinesis Firehose, FluentD, Prometheus.
- Top-level streams give you central destinations — /logs, /metrics, /traces — and sub-streams handle schema and routing underneath.
- The word that matters here is zero-configuration. The pipeline organizes itself.
streams-demo.html:
- Quick demo: the visual pipeline builder.
- Route, enrich, and filter data in real time — no YAML required.
- Watch how fast a non-expert can reshape a pipeline. That used to be a platform team ticket.
signals-intro.html:
- Pillar two: Signals. Every observability experience on one platform.
- Logs: LogsDB, 65% smaller storage, ES|QL for ad-hoc queries, pattern analysis.
- Metrics: Prometheus-native, columnar storage, 30× faster than Prometheus, PromQL in Kibana.
- Traces, synthetics, profiles — same platform, same query language, one bill.
- One platform isn't a slogan; it's a TCO argument.
logs-pitch.html:
- Logs is where we're strongest — and we re-engineered it anyway. Three compounding bets.
- LogsDB index mode, GA since 8.17: smart sorting puts similar records next to each other, synthetic _source stops storing fields twice.
- Net: 65% storage reduction versus standard Elasticsearch. 50% TCO reduction.
- When someone asks why Elastic is cheaper for logs — this slide is the answer.
columnar.html:
- This slide mirrors the doc-store slide deliberately: logs are messy and schemaless, so we built an engine that extracts and indexes everything. Metrics are the opposite — tiny, identical, relentless — so we built the opposite engine.
- The mechanism: each field is its own column on disk. avg(cpu_usage) touches the cpu_usage column and nothing else — one sequential pass, zero wasted reads. That is a column-based read instead of a full-document scan. That is why columnar is so great for time-series, well-structured data. Physics, not caching tricks.
- DIM filters: proprietary IP. Dimension-aware skip filters pushed down to the storage layer — non-matching blocks are skipped before they are ever decoded. The audience does not need to understand what a DIM filter is; they need to register that Elastic has built something special here. Just say it: this is significant IP.
- Why faster than ClickHouse, who is also columnar? ClickHouse is a full BI engine — all of SQL, joins, OLAP. That generality has a cost on every query. Our engine does one thing: time-series. Purpose-built beats general-purpose in its own domain.
- How storage reached 3.75 bytes per point (from the engineering deep-dive, for questions): doc-value skippers replace inverted indices and BKD trees, giving true columnar files; synthetic _id (tsid + timestamp) means the _id is computed, not stored; trimmed sequence numbers; numeric codecs with 512-byte blocks tuned for dimension patterns like IP addresses; shard routing and index sort on _tsid keeps each series sequential on disk so codecs and skippers stay effective.
- How queries got fast (same source): the TS command aggregates per time series then groups — expresses time-series math in one ES|QL pipeline; sorted _tsid + time enables vectorized, parallel, sequential column reads; zero-copy primitive blocks; time and dimension filters pushed down to Lucene skippers; RATE() computed on ordered slices with correct counter-reset handling.
- On ingest: be honest. Prometheus/Glyphos is approximately 10-20% faster at ingest than we are. Saying this buys credibility — then you explain that query and storage are where the cost and pain live, and there we lead by a wide margin.
- For the full technical detail, reference the architectural improvements and benchmark comparison blog (Alex Batsakis's team).
promql.html:
- 80% of enterprise SREs already speak PromQL. That's their language — we didn't ask them to learn ours.
- 90% of queries in the top 100 Grafana dashboards execute natively in Kibana today.
- No plugins, no adapters, no translation layer — it runs wherever ES|QL runs.
- The framing: everything they know, everything they've built — same queries, up to 30× faster.
migrate.html:
- Migration risk is the objection that kills deals. This neutralizes it.
- Three steps: connect Datadog or Grafana, automatic conversion of dashboards and alert rules, go live in Kibana.
- Overnight. Not a quarter-long services engagement.
- The team keeps their workflows; only the backend changes.
kubernetes.html:
- 93% of companies are running or evaluating Kubernetes — that's the universe this lands in. (Source: CNCF 2024 Annual Survey.)
- Out of the box: revamped dashboards and alerts, OOTB SLOs, enhanced OTel experience, agent skills for K8s workflows.
- No instrumentation project, no dashboard-building sprint. It's just there on day one.
- That's what a lovable OOTB experience means — value before configuration.
plain-english.html:
- This is where observability becomes conversational.
- Native MCP server: connect any Claude-compatible client directly to the Elastic cluster.
- Skills load automatically — significant events, RCA, anomaly detection, remediation. Results render as rich cards, not raw JSON.
- Talk to your systems in plain English, inside the agents and workflows your teams already use.
mcp-demo.html:
- The framing on this one matters: engineers already live in an agent. We don't pull them into another tool — we meet them in theirs.
- The demo plays by itself — the chat drives the app. Watch the sequence: connect to the cluster, and six observability skills load automatically from the MCP server. That's the injection story: no custom engineering per use case, skills are discovered at handshake.
- Then the conversation: health summary, ML-scored anomaly explorer, root-cause drill-down, blast radius — each question renders live in the panel.
- No dashboard hunting, no query writing, no context switch. 'What's wrong with my cluster?' — and it answers with data.
- This is shipping, not a concept demo. (Arrow keys skip/rewind if you need to pace it.)
ns-intro.html:
- Beat. Let the name land.
- Elastic nightshift. The shift nobody wants to work — the one that starts when your team goes home.
nightshift-intro.html:
- Pillar three: Elastic nightshift, the autonomous AI SRE. On shift around the clock, so your engineers are not.
- The four capabilities read as a flow, left to right.
- Detect: ML anomaly detection, alert correlation and dedup, blast radius scoring. It ranks incidents by impact before a human is paged.
- Investigate: a parallel hypothesis engine pulling context from every signal (logs, metrics, traces), findings ranked by evidence strength.
- Remediate: proposes and executes fixes at the trust level you define, with rollback safety.
- Audit: every step cited, logged, and explainable. A full compliance trail from trigger to resolution.
- The trust strip is the objection killer: autonomy is configurable. Suggest is read-only, Confirm keeps a human in the loop, Auto is fully autonomous. Every action is audited and reversible regardless of level.
- Numbers if asked: 24/7 coverage, zero on-call pages, unbounded parallel hypotheses.
05-ai-driven.html:
- The strategy behind Elastic nightshift: agentic observability, three moves.
- Infer knowledge from telemetry: technologies, entities, and relationships detected automatically — no config toil.
- Discover significant events: stitch alerts into a complete incident picture before the business feels it.
- Remediate with human in the loop.
- Logs carry context, metrics carry state, traces carry both. The signals were always there — now something reads them.
07-ki-demo.html:
- Knowledge Indicators — this is the auto-detection engine in Streams.
- Entities: services, databases, technologies detected from log patterns. Dependencies: service-to-service relationships inferred from call patterns. Schema: ECS mappings applied automatically.
- No configuration, no instrumentation. The system learns your architecture from the data you already send.
- This is the raw material everything downstream builds on.
system-model.html:
- Those knowledge indicators roll up into the Live System Model — built continuously from telemetry, always current.
- During an incident the agent navigates this model: traverses dependencies, measures impact, isolates the root cause.
- Auto-updated seconds ago — not a CMDB that was stale the day it shipped.
- This is how the agent reasons about your system instead of just querying it.
08-discovery.html:
- Discovery: from raw events to a Significant Event.
- Left side: the noise — OOM exceptions, latency spikes, pod restarts, error spikes. Individually meaningless.
- Discovery correlates them, runs root-cause analysis, scores blast radius — and produces one fully-understood operational situation.
- Alert fatigue dies here: instead of fifty pages, one significant event with the story already assembled.
arcs-option-b.html:
- Elastic nightshift operates across three arcs — think of them as the surfaces where it works.
- Developer arc: code quality and delivery — from Sentry error to merged fix, perf regression to commit, safe deploy rollouts.
- Reliability arc: incident operations — alert to resolution, RCA, triage, SLO burn to mitigation.
- Infrastructure arc: resource efficiency — cost, scale, and drift under control.
- Same agent, same context layer — three domains of action.
nightshift-hero.html:
- Meet your AI SRE. Always watching, always learning, always ready.
- What's on screen is a real incident resolution: detected at 3:47 AM, root cause found, fix applied. Zero human pages.
- Connect your data. The rest takes care of itself.
- That's not a future state — that's the product.
nightshift-architecture.html:
- Under the hood — walk the layers.
- It starts with your Elastic cluster. On top: the agent layer — significant events, blast radius, alert triage, RCA, correlation, remediation, runbook execution, approval workflows, post-incident review.
- Below: the Context Layer — self-updating failure signatures, fix outcomes, pattern library.
- And it connects to the tools you already use — GitHub, Slack, Jira, PagerDuty. Elastic nightshift sits on top of your stack, it doesn't replace it.
nightshift-capabilities.html:
- Two things to take from this slide.
- Distribution: published where engineers actually work. Every capability ships API-first — Kibana, IDE extensions, CLI, Slack, CI pipelines, and AI agents are all equal consumers.
- Action connectors: when Elastic nightshift decides to act, it reaches into Ansible, Terraform, ArgoCD, ServiceNow.
- Investigation and remediation, end to end, wherever your team lives.
nightshift-ai-index.html:
- The Context Layer sits above every observability stack — including ones that aren't ours.
- It connects to the monitoring tools and data stores already in your environment — no migration required.
- What accumulates: failure signatures, fix outcomes, knowledge indicators, the system model, a pattern library.
- Intelligence built from every telemetry source you own. It sits above your stack, not inside it.
nightshift-brain.html:
- One of the most important design decisions: what's yours, what's shared.
- Your brain: your resolved incidents, investigation notes, service topology, system model. Private, trained on your environment.
- Optionally — one opt-in — you contribute anonymized failure signatures to the shared network. No names, no values, no topology. Just the pattern.
- Redis pool exhaustion looks the same at a fintech and a retailer. Your data never leaves; the knowledge does. Everyone gets smarter together.
nightshift-ai-economics.html:
- Why this is economically viable when other AI SRE approaches aren't: token efficiency.
- You cannot pass petabytes of raw telemetry to an LLM. So we don't.
- Raw telemetry stays in low-cost storage, queried on demand via ES|QL. The KI extractor distills it into knowledge indicators, then significant events. Kilobytes reach the model, not gigabytes.
- The platform that compresses signal without losing meaning wins — on quality and on cost.
ns-clickthrough-demo.html:
- Interactive walkthrough of the Elastic nightshift experience — this is the actual product UI.
- Click through at your own pace: incident list, investigation view, evidence, remediation.
- Let the audience direct: pick the incident they'd want to see.
nightshift-live-demo.html:
- Live demo — Elastic nightshift working the incident end to end.
- Watch the sequence: anomaly detected, events grouped into a significant event, blast radius scored HIGH, remediation surfaced.
- Modes on the right: chat, background agent, agent client — same intelligence in every one.
- Elastic nightshift monitors while your team rests. This is what that actually looks like.
nightshift-reveal.html:
- Wake up to this. Not a page — a resolution.
- Incident at 3:43 AM: memory exhaustion in payment-service, cascading to three dependent services. Root cause: Redis connection pool exhaustion. Fixed, verified healthy, by 3:47.
- Zero pages. Zero 3am calls. One full explanation, ready when you are.
- You are not buying observability. You are buying the end of on-call. Let that be the line they remember.
thank-you.html:
- Thank you.
- Three takeaways: Streams gets every signal in at any scale. Signals unifies every experience on one platform, cheaper and faster. Elastic nightshift ends the 3am page.
- Questions welcome — and everything we covered is at elastic.co/observability.
launch.html:
- The headline: Observability Metrics is GA. June 29, 2026.
- Our philosophy: engineers don't change tools — we meet them where they are.
- Three numbers to remember: 30× faster queries than Prometheus. 4× lower TCO than Datadog. Zero dashboard rewrites.
- Grafana dashboards, PromQL queries, alerting rules — all kept. Elastic just becomes the backend underneath.
what-are-metrics.html:
- Quick level-set before the architecture story. Metrics are what wake engineers up at 3am — the highest-frequency signal in observability.
- Three primitives, unchanged since Prometheus: counters only go up, gauges snapshot a point in time, histograms give you p50/p95/p99 from one metric.
- Every alert that fires, every dashboard that renders — it's these three types underneath.
- Hold onto that: three simple types. The next slide shows what AI does to them.
ai-metrics.html:
- Same three types — but AI changes the volume equation completely.
- COUNTER (agent_tool_calls_total): one user query triggers an unknown number of tool calls. Each invocation adds to the count — a staircase that climbs as the agent works. The total is unpredictable until the session ends.
- GAUGE (active_agent_loops): how deep is the agent looping right now? Unlike a web request with a fixed call stack, agents recurse, retry, and branch. Tracking live loop depth is a new instrumentation problem that traditional observability never had to handle.
- HISTOGRAM (tool_response_duration_seconds): web search, code execution, database queries — each tool has its own latency distribution and p50/p95/p99. One histogram per tool type, and agents use many tools. That cardinality alone multiplies your series count.
- The explosion: each AI session spawns new metric dimensions — agent ID, model version, tool name, retry count. As adoption scales, the series count explodes. Most standard metric stores charge per series.
- The blindness risk: incident investigation depends on the full chain of events across every agent call, tool invocation, and model response. Drop a metric series — even one — and you lose the thread. Missing data is not a gap; it is a blind spot that makes RCA impossible.
- These two problems — cost and blindness — are why the architecture had to change.
doc-store.html:
- This slide is a standalone celebration of the doc store — do not frame it as a 'before.' Elastic's document store is still the right architecture for logs. This is not a history lesson.
- How it works: any log line — JSON, syslog, unstructured app log — comes in. Fields are extracted automatically, regardless of schema. An inverted index is built: 'ERROR' maps to doc0, doc3, doc7... 'payment-svc' maps to doc0, doc1, doc2... Any new field is indexed automatically — no schema migration, no DDL.
- Why this beats ClickHouse for logs: Elastic does MATCH and SCORE. ClickHouse does match but not score, and its match on unstructured data is significantly slower. Application logs — arbitrary schema, constantly evolving — are where Elastic is untouchable. Most engineering teams will never put application logs into ClickHouse. ClickHouse works on standardized structured logs; it doesn't handle the messy reality of app logs.
- The main point to land: Elastic made inverted indexes work at log scale. That is real engineering. You do not need to apologize for this architecture — it is genuinely great at what it does.
columnar-intro.html:
- Let this one land on its own: 25 bytes per data point down to 3.75.
- The transition line into this slide, spoken over the doc-store slide: 'Now, what happens when you put a metric into that document store? A metric is tiny — a timestamp, a value, a few dimensions. But the doc store wraps it in machinery built for documents: an _id, sequence numbers, inverted index entries, per-field metadata. You are storing all that metadata for something so small. And reading it back means scanning the full document — effectively a full table scan.'
- Then this number lands: we got it down to 3.75 bytes per point. (Slide auto-advances into the columnar engine slide.)
benchmarks.html:
- The claim to open with, per Ash: we built the best data store for logs. We believe we have now done it for metrics.
- The question this slide preempts: 'how did you become 30× faster than Prometheus? What did you do?' Every number has its how on the slide. Be ready to go one level deeper on each.
- Queries (30× vs Prometheus and Mimir; up to 8× vs ClickHouse on gauges, 3.5× on counter rates): series sorted on disk by _tsid then time; one column read; DIM filters and doc-value skippers eliminate non-matching blocks before they are decoded; single vectorized aggregation pass (the TS command in ES|QL). Concrete anchor on the slide: 4 hours over 1.4M series in under 2s vs over 30s for Prometheus.
- Storage (3.75 bytes per point, 6.7× vs ES 8.x, 2.5× vs Prometheus, 2× vs ClickHouse): store less, compute the rest. Synthetic _id derived from tsid + timestamp instead of stored; doc-value skippers replace inverted indices and BKD trees; trimmed sequence numbers; numeric codec blocks widened from 128 to 512 elements to catch repeating dimension patterns like IPs.
- Ingest: parity with Prometheus and Mimir (the benchmark actually shows us slightly ahead, by a small margin), 1.4× faster than ClickHouse. Do not oversell this one; conceding it is the credibility play. How: native OTLP protobuf parsing (cheaper than JSON), _tsid hash computed once per batch and amortized, synthetic recovery source halves ingest disk IO.
- Methodology if pressed: default configurations for every system (Prometheus v3.11.1, Mimir v3.0.6, ClickHouse v26.3), open-source workload generator (metricsgenreceiver, inspired by TSBS), disclosed EC2 hardware, single-node. Multi-node scale-out results are planned for a future post.
- Caveat to volunteer if asked about ClickHouse queries: ClickHouse lacks native time-series aggregations and counter-reset detection, so those comparisons are directional.
- Source: Elastic Search Labs blog, 'Elasticsearch columnar metrics engine: 30x faster than Prometheus'.
one-platform.html:
- This is the slide Santosh asked for: single platform, yet optimized per signal. The third repetition of the visual pattern (doc store slide, columnar slide, now this) is deliberate: we keep building the right engine for each signal, and the user never feels the seams.
- The routing point: depending on the signal, Elasticsearch uses a different index type automatically. Nobody configures 'send logs here, metrics there.' It just happens. Zero config.
- The three engines: document store (match and score for logs), columnar store (one column read for metrics), vector store (semantic similarity for meaning: incident reports, runbooks, embeddings).
- The payoff on the right: one question touches all three. 'Why is checkout slow?' correlates a metric spike (columnar), the error logs (doc store), and a similar past incident with a documented fix (vector). No other platform answers that in one query, because signals live in separate products with separate query languages.
- Ash's framing to carry verbally: this is super cool because it is the same query mechanism, same dashboards, everything, and each signal is hyper optimized underneath.
- This leads into the next slide: the platform is the foundation, and on top of it we ship a full solution for metrics, not just a data store.
challenge.html:
- The story in one visual: observability was already hard (microservices, multi-cloud, cost: the flat part of the curve). Then AI arrived, and the curve went vertical.
- The three annotations, following the software lifecycle: development, x100, swarms of agents committing code no one has read. Staging, x10, agents provisioning environments no one tracks. Production, unknown multiplier, incidents on code with zero tribal knowledge and no runbook.
- The y-axis is everything at once: telemetry volume, incident count, and the observability bill. They all ride the same curve.
- The punchline sets up the rest of the deck: observability built for humans cannot keep up. That is why the answer is AI-driven observability, not more dashboards.
ns-msg-investigate.html:
- Priority message 1: investigates like an SRE, shows you how it got there. Alt framing: gets smarter with every incident.
- Why this matters: few incident investigations look exactly the same. To be effective, AI needs to learn how to actually think like an SRE: which thread to pull, what is connected, how to go deeper, when to rule something out, and apply that expertise at scale.
- How: Elastic nightshift learns how to investigate, not just what to look for. It traverses the causal chain like an SRE would, tests multiple hypotheses in parallel, and converges on the root cause with reasoning made transparent.
- Over time it learns from how it got there, expanding expertise with every incident, to deliver evidence-backed remediation you can trust.
- The diagram walks a real example: three hypotheses tested in parallel, two ruled out with the reason shown, root cause confirmed, 14 steps all cited.
ns-msg-context.html:
- Priority message 2: complete context, not just what you could afford to keep. Alt framing: built on the broadest investigation context.
- Why: context is the limiting factor for investigation quality. It is often dropped to control costs, or fragmented across telemetry, code repos, runbooks, past incidents, Slack.
- How: Elastic nightshift gives the agent context no other platform can match, from four sources.
- One: telemetry stored in full with best-in-class storage efficiency (this connects back to the metrics/storage story earlier in the deck).
- Two: investigation memory that compounds with every incident.
- Three: deep code understanding, connecting code to telemetry.
- Four: precise, relevant organizational knowledge retrieved from the broadest corpus in the industry.
ns-msg-unknowns.html:
- Priority message 3: finds unknown issues before they find you. Alt framing: detects the blind spots alerts cannot cover.
- Why: AI introduces unknown failure modes you cannot anticipate and cannot write alerts for. SREs are drowning in noise while often missing what actually matters.
- How: Elastic nightshift does not wait for an alert to take action. Ready to go from day one, it continuously surfaces what needs attention, including unknown unknowns, with no configuration required.
- The visual: the dashed box is your alert coverage (the known failure modes). The amber dots outside it are real issues no alert existed for: a token spend anomaly, a silent retry storm, a slow leak, an agent loop runaway. That outside region is where AI-era incidents live.
ns-msg-anywhere.html:
- Priority message 4: deploy anywhere, wherever your data lives.
- Why: many AI SREs are cloud-only. For organizations with strict data residency requirements, air-gapped environments, or regulatory constraints, that is not an option.
- How: Elastic nightshift meets you where you are. Cloud, on-premises, or fully air-gapped: the same investigative capabilities work across all deployment models without architectural compromise.
- Federated queries mean data can be queried anywhere it already lives.
- No data leaves your environment unless you decide it does. Security posture stays intact. Compliance requirements stay met.
ns-msg-plugplay.html:
- Priority message 5 (added per Baha): zero-friction adoption. Elastic nightshift plugs into the customer environment as it exists today, not only an Elastic environment.
- The flow: deploy, connect your alert sources, and investigations start the same day. No migration project first.
- Alerting: PagerDuty, Alertmanager, Opsgenie, or any webhook. The customer alerts they already have become investigation triggers.
- Telemetry: federated queries reach Prometheus, CloudWatch, OTel and more, where the data already lives. Elasticsearch is not a prerequisite; it is where they can consolidate later for the deepest context.
- Knowledge: GitHub, Confluence, Slack, Jira. Runbooks and incident history are read from the tools the team already uses.
- The strategic point: this is the wedge. Nightshift lands on top of whatever they run, proves value on day one, and pulls the rest of the platform behind it on the customer terms.
